title: Asian Americans Use Anxiety Medication at Half the Rate of White Americans. The Reasons Go Deeper Than Stigma.
excerpt: A national study of 29,000 adults found that Asian Americans with diagnosed anxiety disorders are 45 per cent less likely to take medication than their white peers. For the South Asian diaspora, the data confirms a crisis hiding in plain sight.
body:
The numbers are blunt. Among Americans who have been diagnosed with an anxiety disorder, 64.3 per cent of white adults take medication. Among Asian Americans with the same diagnosis, only 45.1 per cent do. That is not a cultural preference. It is a treatment gap with measurable health consequences.

A new study published in Frontiers in Public Health, drawing on data from the 2023 National Health Interview Survey of nearly 30,000 adults, quantified what many South Asian families have long felt but rarely discussed: that even when the diagnosis is made, the community is less likely to follow through with treatment.

The Data, Unpacked

After adjusting for age, income, education, insurance status, and the severity of anxiety, Asian Americans still had 45 per cent lower odds of using anxiety medication compared to white Americans. The gap was not explained by access or affordability. It persisted across income levels, though higher-income Asian Americans were somewhat more likely to take medication than their lower-income peers.

Perhaps the most telling finding was the age curve. Among white Americans, anxiety medication use increases steadily with age — older adults are more likely to be medicated. Among Asian Americans, the opposite was true. Medication use declined with age, suggesting that older generations are the least likely to accept pharmacological treatment, even when it has been prescribed.

The South Asian Layer

The study grouped all Asian Americans together, but for the South Asian diaspora specifically, the dynamics are layered.

Start with language. First-generation Indian, Pakistani, and Bangladeshi immigrants may describe anxiety as "tension" or "overthinking" rather than a clinical condition. The vocabulary for mental illness in Hindi, Urdu, Tamil, or Bengali often carries connotations of madness — pagalpan — rather than a treatable chemical imbalance.

Then there is the family architecture. In joint-family cultures, the expectation is that family support should be sufficient. Seeking outside help — particularly medication — can feel like an admission that the family has failed. The phrase that echoes through consulting rooms serving South Asian patients is some version of "we handle things within the family."

And then there is the professional cost. South Asian Americans are disproportionately represented in fields — medicine, law, finance, technology — where disclosing a mental health condition or a prescription for psychiatric medication carries real or perceived career risk.

What Happens When You Don't Treat

Untreated anxiety is not a minor inconvenience. It is a cardiovascular risk factor. A 2025 meta-analysis in the European Heart Journal found that generalised anxiety disorder is associated with a 26 per cent increased risk of coronary heart disease and a 48 per cent increased risk of cardiac death. For South Asians, who already face the highest heart-disease risk of any ethnic group in the United States, untreated anxiety compounds an already elevated baseline.

Anxiety also worsens metabolic health. It increases cortisol, which increases visceral fat, which increases insulin resistance — the exact metabolic cascade that South Asians are genetically predisposed to. Treating anxiety is not separate from treating the community's cardiovascular crisis. It is part of the same problem.

What Is Working

The data is not entirely grim. Younger South Asian Americans show significantly more willingness to engage with mental health treatment. The rise of South Asian therapists on social media — many of whom speak directly to the cultural barriers — has helped normalise the conversation in ways that clinical outreach never did.

Organisations like the South Asian Mental Health Initiative and the Desi Mental Health Collective have built referral networks of culturally competent therapists who understand the specific pressures of immigrant families, model-minority expectations, and intergenerational dynamics.

Some primary care physicians in heavily South Asian areas have started screening for anxiety during routine visits, framing medication as no different from blood pressure or cholesterol treatment. The reframing matters. When anxiety medication is presented as a cardiovascular intervention rather than a psychiatric one, compliance improves.

The Conversation That Needs to Happen

The study's authors note that their Asian American subsample was small, and they call for larger, disaggregated studies that separate South Asian, East Asian, and Southeast Asian populations. The mental health profiles of these communities are different, and lumping them together obscures the specific barriers each faces.

For the South Asian diaspora, the message is straightforward. If you have been diagnosed with an anxiety disorder and you are not taking medication because of what your parents might think, or because you believe you should be able to handle it, or because you think medication is for people who are weak — the data says you are not alone. Nearly 55 per cent of Asian Americans with diagnosed anxiety are in the same position.

The data also says the cost of that decision is not just psychological. It is metabolic, cardiovascular, and measurable.

Sources: Frontiers in Public Health (2026), doi: 10.3389/fpubh.2026.1803386; European Heart Journal (2025); National Health Interview Survey (2023); JAHA MASALA cohort (2026)
